SOURCE: "Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey on Agentic RAG", Aditi Singh, Abul Ehtesham, Saket Kumar, Tala Talaei Khoei, Athanasios V. Vasilakos; preprint, arXiv:2501.09136v4 [cs.AI], dated 1 Apr 2026 (this version; first posted Jan 2025). Companion repo: github.com/asinghcsu/AgenticRAG-Survey.
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/sources/singh-2025-agentic-retrieval-augmented-generation.pdf

COVERAGE: 114,912 of 114,912 chars; all 42 pages read (body pp. 1-36, references pp. 36-42 skimmed for origins). Nothing skipped. Figures are images only (no text extracted from them); captions listed below.

CLAIMS
Headline: this is a purely narrative survey. It reports NO experiments, NO benchmark numbers, NO quantitative results of its own, and it does not reproduce numbers from the papers it cites. The only numerals in the body are (a) made-up "Integrated Response" strings inside illustrative use cases (e.g. "20% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions", "15% growth over the past quarter", "50% correlation between diabetes and heart disease", invoice "$15,000.00 ... 2% ... 5%") which are fictional example outputs, not findings, and (b) benchmark descriptions ("BEIR ... across 17 datasets", "RAGBench ... 100,000 examples"). Do not cite any of these as results.

- claim: The survey's taxonomy dimensions are agent cardinality, control structure, autonomy and knowledge representation.
  number: none
  setup: survey framing, p.1 abstract and p.36 conclusion
  quote: "introduces a principled taxonomy of Agentic RAG architectures based on agent cardinality, control structure, autonomy, and knowledge representation"
  where: p.1

- claim: Taxonomy (Section 5, pp.14-28), one-line definitions, each with a worked "use case" and a "Key Features / Challenges" list:
  * Single-Agent Agentic RAG: Router (5.1, p.14): "a centralized decision-making system where a single agent manages the retrieval, routing, and integration of information"; routes among Text-to-SQL for structured DBs, semantic/vector search, web search, recommendation systems. "particularly effective for setups with a limited number of tools or data sources." Credited to [32] Weaviate blog.
  * Multi-Agent Agentic RAG (5.2, p.16): "distributes responsibilities across multiple agents, each optimized for a specific role or data source"; coordinator/master retrieval agent delegates to Agent 1 SQL, Agent 2 semantic search, Agent 3 web, Agent 4 recommendations, run in parallel. Challenges: "Coordination Complexity", "Computational Overhead", "Data Integration". Credited to [32].
  * Hierarchical Agentic RAG (5.3, p.18): "Agents are organized in a hierarchy, with higher-level agents overseeing and directing lower-level agents"; top-tier agent assesses complexity and prioritizes sources, delegates, aggregates. Credited to [15] Ravuru et al. 2024 (time-series agentic RAG).
  * Agentic Corrective RAG (5.4, pp.19-21): "introduces mechanisms to self-correct retrieval results"; five agents: Context Retrieval, Relevance Evaluation (documents "below the relevance threshold trigger corrective steps"; classified "relevant, ambiguous, or irrelevant"), Query Refinement, External Knowledge Retrieval (web search when context insufficient), Response Synthesis. Credited to [33] Yan et al. CRAG 2024 and [34] LangGraph CRAG tutorial.
  * Adaptive Agentic RAG (5.5, pp.21-23): "employs a classifier to assess query complexity and determine the most appropriate approach, ranging from single-step retrieval to multi-step reasoning, or even bypassing retrieval altogether for straightforward queries"; "A smaller language model analyzes the query to predict its complexity. The classifier is trained using automatically labeled datasets, derived from past model outcomes and query patterns." Credited to [35] Jeong et al. Adaptive-RAG 2024 and [36] LangGraph tutorial.
  * Graph-Based Agentic RAG (5.6, pp.23-27): Agent-G [8] Lee et al. 2024 ("integrates graph knowledge bases with unstructured document retrieval"; retriever bank + critic module + feedback loops) and GeAR [37] Shen et al. 2024 ("Graph Expansion: Enhances conventional base retrievers (e.g., BM25) by expanding the retrieval process to include graph-structured data").
  * Agentic Document Workflows (5.7, pp.27-28): LlamaIndex ADW [38]; "maintaining state, coordinating multi-step workflows, and applying domain-specific logic to documents"; parse (LlamaParse) -> state -> retrieve -> orchestrate -> structured output.
  number: none
  setup: conceptual descriptions; no evaluation
  quote: "These include single-agent architectures, multi-agent systems, and hierarchical agentic architectures."
  where: p.14

- claim: Four agentic design patterns: Reflection, Planning, Tool Use, Multi-Agent (Section 3, pp.9-11), credited to [26] Singh et al. 2024 and [27] DeepLearning.AI (Andrew Ng's "How agents can improve LLM performance"). Reflection: "prompting an agent to critique its outputs for correctness, style, and efficiency, then incorporating this feedback into subsequent iterations"; cites Self-Refine [28], Reflexion [29], CRITIC [24]. Planning: "can produce less predictable outcomes compared to deterministic workflows like Reflection". Tool Use: mentions "GPT-4's function calling capabilities" and that tool selection among many tools can use "heuristic-based selection". Multi-Agent: "a less predictable design pattern compared to more mature workflows like Reflection and Tool Use"; names AutoGen, Crew AI, LangGraph.
  number: none
  where: pp.9-11

- claim: Five agentic workflow patterns (Section 4, pp.11-14), credited to [13] Anthropic "Building effective agents" (2024) and [31] LangGraph workflows tutorial: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization (sectioning and voting), orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer. Each has a "When to Use" line.
  number: none
  where: pp.11-14

- claim: Traditional RAG vs Agentic RAG vs ADW comparison (Table 2, p.29). Rows: Focus / Context Maintenance / Dynamic Adaptability / Workflow Orchestration / Use of External Tools/APIs / Scalability / Complex Reasoning / Primary Applications / Strengths / Challenges. Traditional: "Isolated retrieval and generation tasks", context "Limited", adaptability "Minimal", orchestration "Absent", scalability "Limited to small datasets or queries", reasoning "Basic (e.g., simple Q&A)", strengths "Simplicity, quick setup", challenges "Poor contextual understanding". Agentic: "Multi-agent collaboration and reasoning", context "Enabled through memory modules", adaptability "High", "Orchestrates multi-agent tasks", "Scalable for multi-agent systems", "Multi-step reasoning with agents", strengths "High accuracy, collaborative reasoning", challenges "Coordination complexity". ADW: "Document-centric end-to-end workflows", "Maintains state across multi-step workflows", applications "Contract review, invoice processing, claims analysis", challenges "Resource overhead, domain standardization".
  number: none (qualitative table)
  where: p.29

- claim: Taxonomy-driven comparison (Table 3, p.33) with dimensions Agent Cardinality, Control Structure, Knowledge Representation, Knowledge Dependency, Reasoning Mode, Reasoning Depth, Retrieval Adaptivity, Scalability, Latency, Engineering Complexity, Best-Fit Scenarios across Single-Agent / Multi-Agent / Hierarchical-Corrective / Graph-Based-Document-Centric. Latency row: "Low | Moderate | High | Moderate to high". Engineering complexity: "Low | Moderate | High | High". Best fit: "Simple QA and routing | Multi-domain synthesis | High-stakes, reliability-critical tasks | Knowledge-intensive, relational domains".
  quote: "Single-agent architectures favor simplicity and low latency but struggle with multi-domain reasoning. Multi-agent systems improve scalability through parallelism at the cost of coordination overhead. Hierarchical and corrective architectures enhance reliability through strategic oversight but incur higher latency. Graph-based systems enable structured relational reasoning while introducing dependencies on knowledge quality."
  where: p.32 (9.1), table p.33

- claim: Lessons learned (Section 10, pp.32-34), the closest the paper gets to "when to use/avoid":
  10.1 "Agentic RAG Is Not Always the Right Default": "For simple fact retrieval or well-scoped queries, modular RAG pipelines provide sufficient performance with lower overhead. Practitioners should adopt agentic designs selectively, guided by task complexity." (p.32)
  10.2 "corrective workflows improve accuracy but add latency, while adaptive architectures trade correctness guarantees for responsiveness." (p.33)
  10.3 "Retrieval Quality Remains the Primary Bottleneck": "Agentic reasoning cannot compensate for consistently poor retrieval. ... Investing in robust retrieval pipelines and high-quality indexing before introducing agentic complexity remains essential." (p.33)
  10.4 "Agent Autonomy Requires Explicit Constraints": "Unrestricted autonomy risks excessive tool invocation, redundant reasoning loops, or misaligned objectives. Effective systems balance autonomy with bounded planning horizons, predefined tool access policies, and explicit stopping criteria." (p.33)
  10.5 "Evaluation Must Account for Process, Not Just Outcomes": "Meaningful evaluation requires process-level metrics capturing reasoning efficiency, tool usage patterns, and adaptation to changing contexts." (p.33)
  10.6 "Agentic RAG achieves its strongest gains in domains with structured knowledge and explicit constraints. Healthcare, finance, and legal analysis particularly benefit ... Open-domain tasks show more modest gains" (p.33; no evidence cited for this).
  10.7 "Explainability, traceability, and auditability must be first-class design goals, particularly for high-stakes applications." (p.34)
  number: none

- claim: Applications (Section 7, pp.29-31): customer support (Twitch ad sales on Amazon Bedrock [39], AWS blog), healthcare patient case summary [40], legal contract review [41], auto insurance claims [42], education / research paper generation [43] (all [40]-[43] are LlamaCloud demo notebooks), "Graph-Enhanced Agentic RAG (GEAR)" market-survey generation (no citation). All narrative; "significantly boosting operational efficiency" for Twitch is asserted without numbers.
  where: pp.29-31

- claim: Tools (Section 8, pp.31-32): LangChain/LangGraph, LlamaIndex ADW, Hugging Face + Qdrant, CrewAI and AG2 (formerly AutoGen), OpenAI Swarm, Vertex AI, Semantic Kernel, Amazon Bedrock, IBM watsonx.ai (Granite-3-8B-Instruct), Neo4j + Weaviate/Pinecone/Milvus/Qdrant.

- claim: Open challenges (Section 12, pp.34-36): agent coordination and emergent behaviour ("orchestration relies on heuristic rules and prompt engineering with limited convergence guarantees"); evaluation beyond output quality ("Output-level metrics (answer correctness, retrieval accuracy) are insufficient for Agentic RAG"); memory management ("Persistent memory risks knowledge drift and bias reinforcement"); computational cost; safety/trust/governance ("In multi-agent settings, tracing responsibility is particularly challenging"); cross-domain generalization ("Most existing Agentic RAG systems are evaluated in domain-specific settings or carefully curated benchmarks").

- claim: Benchmarks named (Section 11, p.34): BEIR, MS MARCO, TREC DL, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultihopQA, Agent-G, HotpotQA, RAGBench, BERGEN, FlashRAG, GNN-RAG; Table 4/5 (pp.35, 37, duplicated) is a dataset list "Adapted from [21]" (Gao et al. RAG survey).

NOTE-VS-SURVEY CHECK (what the caller asked)
- The note's use/avoid table ("multi-step reasoning", "several sources compared", "accuracy over speed", "provenance non-negotiable", "human-level analysis" vs "one-shot works", "latency critical", "can't afford complex operations", "poor data quality"): NOT in the survey verbatim. In substance, only partially: 10.1 (not the default; use when task complexity warrants), 10.3 (poor retrieval/indexing is the bottleneck, roughly "poor data quality"), 9.1/Table 3 (latency rises with corrective/hierarchical designs). "Provenance", "human-level", "one-shot", "latency is critical" do not occur in the text (grep: 0 hits).
- "Before shipping" checklist (multiple retrieval strategies, planner separate from generator, validation step, traceable evidence, tool use rate-limited, human override paths, metrics beyond answer quality): NOT in the survey as a checklist. Partial substance: 10.4 ("predefined tool access policies, and explicit stopping criteria" ~ rate-limited tool use), 10.7 (human oversight, traceability, auditability), 10.5 (metrics beyond outcomes). "override" and "rate limit" have 0 hits.
- "What to measure" list (retrieval precision, evidence coverage per answer, self-correction rate, human override frequency, time-to-trust): NOT in the survey. "time-to-trust", "self-correction rate", "evidence coverage", "override" all 0 hits; "retrieval precision" appears only twice, both describing dense retrievers (pp.3, 5), not as a metric to track. The survey's own metric suggestion is generic: "process-level metrics capturing reasoning efficiency, tool usage patterns, and adaptation to changing contexts" (p.33) and "reasoning trajectories, planning depth, adaptability, robustness under noisy retrieval, and cost efficiency" (p.34).
- The note's closing lines ("direction of travel is multi-agent collaboration, better self-verification, and personalisation with guardrails"; "makes good systems better and bad ones dangerous"; "Retrieval without judgment is noise; judgment without evidence is hallucination"): NOT in the survey (0 hits for "self-verification", "guardrail", "dangerous", "judgment"). These lists were drawn from somewhere else or written by the note's author; they cannot be attributed to Singh et al.

LIMITS
- No experiments, no reported numbers, no comparison of cited systems' results; every architecture is described with a fictional worked example and invented "Integrated Response" text. Claims like "High accuracy" for Agentic RAG (Table 1 p.8, Table 2 p.29) and "Agentic RAG systems reduce latency through optimized workflows" (p.9) are asserted, not evidenced, and the latter contradicts Table 3's own latency row.
- Heavy reliance on vendor blogs and tutorials as primary sources: Weaviate blog [32] for single/multi-agent taxonomy, LangGraph tutorials [34][36][44], LlamaIndex blog/notebooks [38][40]-[43][45], AWS blog [39], Qdrant/HF cookbooks [46][47]. Several applications are demo notebooks, not deployments.
- Authors concede: "the field remains at an early stage of maturity" (p.34); "Most existing Agentic RAG systems are evaluated in domain-specific settings or carefully curated benchmarks" (p.36); "no single architecture is universally optimal" (p.36).
- Sections 6 and 9 are both titled "Comparative Analysis of Agentic RAG Frameworks" and both point at Table 2; Tables 4 and 5 are near-duplicates. Section 7.6 "GEAR" (market surveys, multimodal) conflates with 5.6.2 GeAR [37] (multi-hop graph retrieval) without a citation.
- Dated: v4 updates the intro to name "GPT-5" and cites 2026 accessed URLs, but the architecture descriptions are unchanged from the Jan 2025 version in substance; OpenAI Swarm is listed though it is an "educational framework".
